1.1: 1.1 Argument. Likewise he writes to Timothy about exhortation to martyrdom, and about every rule of truth, and what will be in the last times, and about his own passion, writing to him from the city of Rome. Paul an apostle. First the Apostle greets, then gives thanks for the good which he has, where he shows his desire to see him. Afterwards he admonishes him to preach, and to patience in martyrdom, by his own example and in other ways. Then he says what sort of men there will be in the last days: finally of the imminent time of his own dissolution. By the will of God. Not by my merits, as if he said: Likewise you also were sent freely, and therefore are the more bound to preach grace.
1.3: 1.3 I give thanks. He gives thanks for his good, commending the grace of the faith which is in Christ. Remembrance. For Timothy wept when dismissed by Paul, ready to go with him to all dangers. What therefore he had when present, let him hold when absent, receiving also the remembrance of the faith that may admonish you, since it was firm even in women.
1.6: 1.6 For which cause. His faith being commended, he exhorts him to preach it without fear and shame. By the imposition of hands. That is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which you received for the establishing of the Church, for working miracles, for every service of religion.
1.7: 1.7 Of fear. Peter, disturbed by fear, denied Christ. Hence: Do not fear those who kill the body, Matthew 26. We have not received the spirit of this fear, but of that of which the Lord says: Fear him who can destroy both body and soul in hell. For the Holy Spirit gives fear not of the world but of God, who can destroy in the hell of fire.
1.8: 1.8 Be not therefore. He teaches that constancy is to be had, and that one is not to be ashamed in the profession: for there is no reason to be ashamed of it: because although Christ was seen as man, yet by his deeds he appeared God; and though he was crucified, yet he rose from the dead, and in the sight of many, a cloud receiving him, he ascended into heaven. Where therefore weakness is supposed, there power appears.
1.9: 1.9 Who has delivered us. It is fitting to repay him who delivers: since we cannot worthily answer his benefits, let us at least faithfully and earnestly carry out his embassy.
1.10: 1.10 Who has destroyed. Death, as conquered, is not to be feared for the faith of Christ. He has enlightened. To what end these things look, there he opens: Having the form. Through the Gospel. God has shown incorruptible life, which was before unknown, shown, I say, through the preaching of the Gospel of which Paul is the preacher.
1.11: 1.11 Whereunto I am appointed. Here he exhorts by his own example. Preacher, and apostle, and teacher, etc. What reason is there, since he continually calls himself teacher of the Gentiles? Doubtless he wishes to persuade that the Gentiles also are called to the inheritance of God, and therefore are not to be repelled from the fellowship of the faith.
1.12: 1.12 For I know. As if he said: Therefore I am not confounded, that is I do not fail, or I do not suffer in vain, because he promised and is truthful and powerful: and therefore I have believed him himself, who will repay me. Because he is able. He is secure by the hope and magnificence of the Savior, because what he commits to him is safe. He commits to him his salvation, that here suffering for him he may find salvation with him when he begins to judge, that punishing the unfaithful he may pronounce this one worthy of eternal life.
1.13: 1.13 Hold the form. Here he shows to what end the aforesaid things regarding himself look. As if he said: So I labor in this office entrusted to me: likewise therefore you also, holding the form, etc. Of whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes. These pretended to be with the Apostle in order to find calumny: but after they saw themselves exposed, they withdrew from him.
2.4: 2.4 No man being a soldier. As if he said: If you wish to be a good soldier, do not entangle yourself in secular business, because no man, etc. Business. Secular business is when the mind is occupied with the care of gathering money without labor of body, like merchants and the like: which lest he do, because being weak he could not labor, he forbids.
2.6: 2.6 The husbandman that laboreth. As if Timothy asked: Whence then shall I live, since I cannot dig, and am ashamed to beg? he adds the husbandman that laboreth. As if he said, though you are not entangled in secular business, there is yet whence you can live: Because it behooves, etc. First to partake. That is, to take. Of the fruits. That is the necessaries from the hearers, because the laborer is worthy of his hire; as the husbandman or vinedresser first tastes the first fruits of his labor, so the Apostle bids him who is first take, and so distribute to the rest. For he ought first to supply his own need from what he has received, and afterwards minister to others from what remains.
2.8: 2.8 Be mindful. Labor as I do, and this in hope of eternal life. He mentions these things not for Timothy's sake, but for the sake of the heretics whom he foresaw would come and deny them.
2.9: 2.9 As an evildoer. Here he notes the insult which was heaped upon him. But the word of God is not bound. As if he said: Though therefore I am bound in body, yet the word of God is not bound: I who do not cease to teach those present by speech, and those absent by letters.
2.10: 2.10 Salvation, etc., with glory, etc. As if he said: You are justified that here you may obtain salvation, and after this life heavenly glory.
2.11: 2.11 It is a faithful saying. It is this, that they shall obtain salvation and glory, for we are dead to the world, as Christ to the old man, and those who endure, that is the martyrs.
2.14: 2.14 Put them in mind of these things. These things which have been foretold, that you may suffer, I remind you. Or, put your own in mind of these things. For it is useful for nothing. Contention that is less steadfast often breeds a scruple. For in contention such things are wont to be put against a polished argument of ill will, so as to move the minds of foolish brethren. Nor can it be but that contention wrings out something said against conscience, so that one loses within in his soul, and comes away a victor outwardly. For no one suffers himself to be conquered, even though he knows that what he hears is true. Among the servants of God there ought to be conference, not wrangling.
2.17: 2.17 Of whom are Hymenaeus and Philetus. He betrayed their names, that he might spiritually be on guard against them, whom he marks out as profane and impious and straying from the truth.
2.18: 2.18 Saying that the resurrection is past already. There are two resurrections. The first is that which takes place in the soul through faith, when one who was dead in unbelief and other sins is made alive by faith and baptism. The other, which will be of bodies, will be on the day of judgment. Of that resurrection which takes place in the soul by faith the Apostle speaks here when he says: Saying that the resurrection, of minds namely, is already made in baptism, and that in faith there will be no resurrection of bodies. All the sects that promise religion concede the resurrection of minds in faith. For otherwise they would not seem worthy of being heard. Wishing therefore to be believed, even all who founded the sect of any false religion could not deny this resurrection of minds, all agreed about it. But the resurrection of bodies many have denied, like these whom the Apostle names.
2.19: 2.19 The Lord knows who are his, etc. That is, he loves and defends those whom he foreknew. In this is noted the foreknowledge by which those whom he foreknew would be conformed to the image of his Son, that is he predestined, called, justified, glorified.
2.20: 2.20 Vessels of gold and silver. For as vessels of wood and clay are of use that the gold and silver may be cleansed, so the wicked profit the advancement of the good. A great house, therefore, is the Church, in which are vessels of gold and silver, that is, the good and faithful and holy servants of God everywhere dispersed and bound together by spiritual unity, living in the same communion of the sacraments. And vessels of wood and clay, that is those who are in the house, so as not to be in the structure of the house, nor in peaceful fellowship, and yet still in body together with the good.
2.23: 2.23 But avoid foolish and unlearned questions. Not all questions are to be avoided, but the trifling ones and those without discipline.
2.24: 2.24 But the servant of the Lord must not wrangle, but be gentle to all. Those who contradict make noise enough. Let not the servant of God then make noise against himself by zeal for quarreling. He did not wish us to fail in correction of the brethren, nor to be eager for strife. For many men, when roused from sleep, want to quarrel, or go back to sleep when they are forbidden to quarrel.
2.25: 2.25 If peradventure God may give them repentance to know the truth. Correction does not profit unless the heavenly physician looks upon it, that is unless he makes each repent of his sin. This repentance is at times hindered by shame and fear of displeasing others, while the opinion of others delights a man more than the righteousness by which each humbles himself in repenting. And therefore not only when repentance is being done, but that it may be done, the mercy of God is necessary. For that Peter might weep bitterly, the Lord looked upon him. And therefore the Apostle says here: May God give them repentance, Matthew 26.
3.2: 3.2 Lovers of themselves. Not of the Lord, like Peter, who, asked three times by the Lord, three times professed that he loved him, saying: You know that I love you. Hence the Lord entrusted to him the feeding of his sheep: because in feeding the sheep true love is shown, if one seeks there not his own things but the things of Christ. From their loving themselves, not God, as from a root arise the evils that follow. Ungrateful. Those are ungrateful who repay evil for good to those who correct them.
3.5: 3.5 Having a form. Because they have the same sacraments with the pious. But the power. Power is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith unfeigned.
3.6: 3.6 Who creep into. For they entered the houses of women, and deceived them.
3.7: 3.7 Ever learning and never attaining to the knowledge, etc. But let us always walk in the way until we come to where the way leads, never remaining in it, until it brings us where we may abide. And so by seeking we press on, and by finding we arrive at something.
3.8: 3.8 Now as Jannes, etc. As if he said: Such seduce: but they always resist the truth. And this is what he says: Now as Jannes, etc. Jannes and Jambres, two brothers, were magicians of Pharaoh. The Apostle did not find their names in the divine books, but in apocryphal ones, from which this is taken. They resisted Moses up to the third sign, in which they failed, saying: This is the finger of God. And as they resisted Moses, so these, namely the heretics, resist me.
3.13: 3.13 But evil men, etc. Such are those who fear to hurt those before whom they speak, who do not prepare for temptations but promise the happiness of this age, which God himself promised us in this age. He foretells labors that will come to the end of the age: you promise prosperity. He, to strengthen your heart, came to suffer, to die, to be smeared with spittle, to be crowned with thorns, to bear reproaches, to drink gall and vinegar, to be nailed to the wood. All these things he bore for you. He strengthens the weak, that when he has believed, he may not hope for the prosperous things of this age; hence: My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.
3.15: 3.15 You have known the holy scriptures, which, etc. He signifies that it greatly profits to have knowledge of the Old Testament, where the person and incarnation of Christ is hinted, which avails for the salvation of men.
4.2: 4.2 Out of season. You act in season, but you will seem out of season to him who does not gladly hear, what yet sometimes profits him. You, however, knowing that what seems to him unseasonable is seasonable for him, hold with a gentle and modest mind your love and care for his health. Reprove in all things. For Timothy he urges a keener patience. To Titus, who was too patient, he urges command.
4.3: 4.3 They will heap to themselves teachers. That is, who will teach what they want. It is a prophecy of the holy apostle, who, foreknowing the future, commands to be urgent in doctrine, that the Church may be prepared against what was to come. For he says there will be such who wish to be taught according to their own desires, that they turn from teachers who are steady and truthful to those who will teach them what they gladly hear, because truth will seem harsh to them, so that, leaving true doctrine, they give themselves to fables.
4.5: 4.5 Do the work of an evangelist. Attesting by work what you preach with the mouth, so that the mouth of the turtledove be turned back to its shoulders, and there be pomegranates and bells on the edges of the hem of the hyacinth tunic.
4.6: 4.6 I am being poured out. We say libare for to taste, to pour out and to sacrifice. Hence delibare, which however is put here for the sacrifice itself, for he calls his passion a libation. For he is sacrificed to God who suffers for righteousness.
4.7: 4.7 I have kept the faith, which is the head of the Christian religion, which cannot be had except by God having mercy, because it is the gift of God; hence elsewhere he says: I obtained mercy, not because I was faithful, but that I might be faithful. For we find the Apostle, without any good merits, indeed with many vices, obtained the grace of God, who renders good for evil. Who, with his passion now drawing near, recounts his good merits, after which he will obtain the crown, who after evil merits obtained grace: which unless it had first been given freely, the crown would not be rendered. His merits therefore are not his as if from himself, that is gotten by himself, but gifts of God.
4.8: 4.8 He will render. For if faith is grace, and eternal life is as it were the reward of faith; it seems that God renders eternal life as a debt to the faithful man to whom he owes it, because he has merited it through faith; but because faith is grace, and eternal life is grace, he will therefore render it through grace. A just judge. Certainly just in rendering good for good, yet because first he is merciful in rendering good for evil; the very justice by which good is rendered for good is not without mercy.
4.13: 4.13 The cloak. CHRYSOSTOM. He calls the cloak here a mantle, etc., down to that there may be no need to receive it from others.
4.14: 4.14 Alexander. This is he of whom he said above that he returned to apostasy, who made the temples of Diana at Athens, and stirred up all against the Apostle. He showed me many evils. CHRYSOSTOM. He who is pressed by some great man, etc., down to that the weaker also may take comfort from this part too.
4.16: 4.16 Defense. He calls the pressure and tribulation brought upon him a defense: tribulation is a defense for Christians, because it defends them on the day of judgment. May it not be laid to their charge. He does not pray for Alexander, who by envy had sinned by attacking brotherhood, but for those who had broken off love but succumbed to fear; he prays that they may be pardoned. For there is great difference between those who sin in this way and those who sin in that.
4.17: 4.17 From the mouth of the lion. Of Nero, from whose hands he was delivered by the Lord, when he came to Rome brought by those who presided over Judea, because he had appealed to Caesar. For when he had come to Rome he remained two years in free custody, afterwards also passed to other nations that were around Rome.
